standards.PEP8: PEP 8 – Style Guide for Python Code

rules.description: Keep module filenames brief and entirely lowercase. An underscore inside the name is fine when it makes a multi-word module easier to read at a glance, but is not required otherwise.
rules.rationale: Lowercase module names keep import statements predictable and avoid case-sensitivity issues across filesystems.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Package and Module Names

_examples.explanation: all-lowercase module name
CapWords used for a module name instead of lowercase

rules.description: Packages follow the same short, all-lowercase style as modules, but underscores are actively avoided at the package level rather than merely optional.
rules.rationale: Short, underscore-free package names are easier to type in import paths and match long-standing PyPI conventions.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Package and Module Names

_examples.explanation: short, all-lowercase, underscore-free package name
underscore in a package name, which PEP 8 discourages

rules.description: By default, name a class using the CapWords style: each word capitalized and concatenated without separators (also known as PascalCase).
rules.rationale: CapWords visually distinguishes types from functions and variables, which use lowercase conventions.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Class Names

_examples.explanation: CapWords class name
snake_case used for a class name instead of CapWords

rules.description: Exceptions are named like any other class, in CapWords, with one addition: if the exception actually represents a genuine error state (rather than, say, a control-flow signal), its name should end in 'Error'.
rules.rationale: The Error suffix lets readers identify exception types at a glance and distinguishes true errors from control-flow-only exceptions.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Exception Names

_examples.explanation: CapWords name with the Error suffix for an error condition
exception class representing an error but missing the Error suffix

rules.description: Functions are named in all-lowercase snake_case; insert underscores between words only where doing so makes the name easier to read, since a short function name needs none.
rules.rationale: A single consistent case style for callables makes function names instantly recognizable and distinguishes them from class names.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Variable Names

_examples.explanation: snake_case function name
camelCase instead of snake_case

rules.description: Method names follow the same lowercase-with-underscores rule as functions.
rules.rationale: Applying the function-naming rule uniformly to methods keeps a class's public interface consistent with the rest of the codebase.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Method Names and Instance Variables

_examples.explanation: snake_case method name
PascalCase used for a method name

rules.description: Variable names follow the same convention as function names: lowercase with underscores separating words.
rules.rationale: Uniform casing for variables and functions avoids arbitrary style decisions and keeps identifiers scannable.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Variable Names

_examples.explanation: snake_case variable name
camelCase instead of snake_case

rules.description: Module-level constants are written entirely in capital letters, with underscores marking the boundaries between words.
rules.rationale: All-caps names flag values that are meant to be treated as fixed, reducing accidental reassignment.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Constants

_examples.explanation: all-caps constant with underscores
camelCase used for a module-level constant

rules.description: The first parameter of an instance method must always be named 'self'; the first parameter of a class method must always be named 'cls'.
rules.rationale: Fixed conventional names for the implicit first argument let readers immediately recognize instance vs. class methods.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Method Arguments

_examples.explanation: instance method's first parameter is named self
first parameter named 'this' instead of the required 'self'

rules.description: If the most natural parameter name happens to clash with a Python reserved word, resolve the clash with one trailing underscore on the name rather than misspelling or shortening it.
rules.rationale: A trailing underscore keeps the parameter's meaning intact instead of obscuring it with an abbreviation.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Function and Method Arguments

_examples.code:
def build_filter(class_, value):
    return {"class": class_, "value": value}
_examples.explanation: trailing underscore avoids clashing with the 'class' keyword

_examples.code:
def build_filter(klass, value):
    return {"class": klass, "value": value}
_examples.explanation: keyword clash avoided by an abbreviation instead of a trailing underscore

rules.description: Instance attributes intended as non-public should carry a single leading underscore; attributes without one are considered part of the public interface.
rules.rationale: A single leading underscore is a widely understood, weak 'internal use' signal that documents intent without enforcing access control.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Method Names and Instance Variables

_examples.explanation: leading underscore marks an internal-use attribute
internal attribute exposed without the leading-underscore convention

rules.description: A double leading underscore (with no trailing underscore) may be used on an attribute to invoke Python's name-mangling mechanism, helping avoid attribute name clashes when the class is subclassed.
rules.rationale: Name mangling is an opt-in mechanism reserved for attributes that genuinely need subclass-clash protection, so it is optional rather than a default rule.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Method Names and Instance Variables

_examples.explanation: double leading underscore invokes name mangling to protect against subclass clashes
trailing double underscore is reserved for magic names and does not trigger mangling

rules.description: Do not choose a bare lowercase L, uppercase O, or uppercase I as a standalone identifier; depending on the font, each can be mistaken for the digit 1 or 0.
rules.rationale: Visually ambiguous single-letter names cause misreadings that are hard to catch in code review.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Names to Avoid

_examples.explanation: clear, unambiguous variable name
single-letter 'l' is easily confused with the digit 1

rules.description: Public instance attributes should be exposed as plain, simply-named attributes with no leading underscore, rather than hidden behind getter/setter accessor methods unless additional behavior is actually needed.
rules.rationale: Plain attribute access is more idiomatic and readable in Python; properties can be introduced later without breaking the public interface.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Naming Conventions — Designing for Inheritance

_examples.explanation: public attributes exposed directly, no accessor boilerplate
needless getter for a simple public data attribute

rules.triggerCondition: the module is public (not prefixed with an underscore) and forms part of the package's API
rules.description: Public modules should have a docstring summarizing their contents. Neither PEP 8 nor PEP 257 mandates a specific docstring markup style (no required Google-, NumPy-, or reST-style sections) — only the high-level convention that it exists and starts with a one-line summary.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Comments — Documentation Strings; PEP 257

_examples.code:
"""Utilities for formatting currency values."""

import re
_examples.explanation: public module opens with a one-line summary docstring
public module has no module-level docstring at all

rules.triggerCondition: the class is public
rules.description: Public classes should have a docstring summarizing the class's behavior; PEP 257 additionally suggests listing public methods and instance variables, but prescribes no required markup syntax for how that content is formatted.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Comments — Documentation Strings; PEP 257

_examples.code:
class Cache:
    """Store recently used items up to a fixed capacity."""
_examples.explanation: public class has a summarizing docstring
public class defined with no docstring

rules.triggerCondition: the function is public
rules.description: Public functions should have a docstring describing their behavior. Per PEP 257 it should cover arguments, return value, side effects, and exceptions where applicable, but no specific markup style (e.g. Google-style Args:/Returns: sections) is mandated by PEP 8 or PEP 257 — the content, not the format, is the requirement.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Comments — Documentation Strings; PEP 257

_examples.explanation: public function documents its behavior in a docstring
public function with no docstring

rules.triggerCondition: the method is public; if the method is non-public (leading underscore) a docstring is optional
rules.description: Public methods should carry a docstring. Docstrings are not necessary for non-public methods, but PEP 8 recommends at least an explanatory comment describing what a non-public method does.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Comments — Documentation Strings

_examples.explanation: non-public method lacks a docstring but has an explanatory comment
non-public method has neither a docstring nor an explanatory comment

rules.triggerCondition: a block comment precedes a block of code
rules.description: Write block comments as full, properly capitalized sentences, prefix each line with a hash and one space, and update them whenever the code they explain changes, since an outdated comment misleads more than an absent one.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Comments — Block Comments

_examples.code:
# Recompute the cache because the configuration file changed.
refresh_cache()
_examples.explanation: block comment is a complete, capitalized sentence with '# ' prefix
missing space after '#' and not a properly capitalized sentence

rules.triggerCondition: an inline comment follows a statement on the same line
rules.description: Reserve inline comments for cases that genuinely need them; keep at least two spaces before the hash, follow it with one space, and use the comment to say something the code alone does not already convey.
rules.sourceSection: PEP 8 § Comments — Inline Comments

_examples.code: retry_count = 0  # reset after a successful connection
_examples.explanation: two spaces before '# ' and a comment that adds real context
only one space before the comment, no space after '#', and it just restates the obvious

rules.description: Every identifier, of any kind, may contain only ASCII letters and digits, plus underscores in the small number of cases the guide calls out separately (e.g. constant names, JUnit test method names). No other characters or diacritics are used even where Java would allow them.
rules.rationale: Restricting identifiers to ASCII keeps code portable and easy to type, read and search across tools, locales and fonts.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.1 (Rules common to all identifiers)

_examples.explanation: plain ASCII identifier
contains a non-ASCII character (é)

rules.description: Field names never encode their scope or type through a prefix or suffix; conventions such as a leading letter to flag a member, static, or constant field, or a trailing underscore, are all out of scope for this style.
rules.rationale: Encoding scope/type in the name duplicates information already visible from the declaration's modifiers and type, adding noise without benefit.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.1 (Rules common to all identifiers)

_examples.explanation: plain field name, no scope-encoding prefix
Hungarian-style 'm' prefix encoding member scope

rules.description: A package name is built entirely from lowercase ASCII letters and digits, with no underscores anywhere, and multi-word segments are simply run together instead of separated.
rules.rationale: All-lowercase package names avoid case-sensitivity mismatches across filesystems and match long-standing Java conventions.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.1 (Package names)

_examples.explanation: all lowercase, words concatenated
mixed case and underscore in package segment

rules.description: Classes use UpperCamelCase and read as a noun or noun phrase. For a class whose whole purpose is testing some other class, form the name by appending 'Test' to that class's own name (a suite covering PaymentGateway becomes PaymentGatewayTest).
rules.rationale: Uniform PascalCase for types lets readers instantly distinguish type names from methods, fields and constants.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.2 (Class names)

_examples.explanation: PascalCase noun-phrase class name
snake_case instead of PascalCase
test class named after class under test plus 'Test' suffix

rules.description: Interface names follow the same UpperCamelCase convention as classes, but unlike classes may be adjective or adjective-phrase names describing a capability, in addition to noun/noun-phrase names.
rules.rationale: Sharing casing with classes keeps all type names visually uniform, while allowing adjective names communicates capability-style interfaces clearly.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.2 (Class names)

_examples.explanation: PascalCase noun-phrase interface name
snake_case instead of PascalCase

rules.description: Not called out as its own bullet, but since an enum declaration is structurally a kind of class declaration in Java, an enum type's name follows the same UpperCamelCase class-naming convention as an ordinary class.
rules.rationale: Treating enum types like classes keeps type-name casing consistent across every kind of type declaration.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.2 (Class names) — extrapolated, not a separate bullet

_examples.explanation: PascalCase enum type name
snake_case instead of PascalCase

rules.description: Methods are named in lowerCamelCase, and the name is usually built around a verb or verb phrase describing what the method does.
rules.rationale: lowerCamelCase visually separates callable behavior from type names (PascalCase) and constants (UPPER_SNAKE_CASE).
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.3 (Method names)

_examples.explanation: lowerCamelCase verb-phrase method name
snake_case instead of lowerCamelCase

rules.description: JUnit test methods get one carve-out from the usual naming rule: an underscore may separate distinct parts of the scenario under test, provided each part on its own still reads as lowerCamelCase.
rules.rationale: Underscore-separated components make a long test-scenario name easier to parse than one run-on camelCase phrase.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.3 (Method names)

_examples.explanation: underscore separates scenario from expected outcome, each part still lowerCamelCase
components are PascalCase, not lowerCamelCase, even though underscore separation is allowed

rules.description: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE is reserved for genuine constants: static final fields whose value and everything it points to stay unchanged after initialization (primitives, Strings, and other deeply immutable types qualify). A static final field pointing at something mutable, like a list a caller can modify or a Logger, does not meet that bar and takes ordinary field casing instead.
rules.rationale: Distinguishing constants from ordinary fields purely by casing signals to readers that the value can never change at runtime.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.4 (Constant names)

_examples.explanation: deeply-immutable static final int named UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
true constant styled in lowerCamelCase instead of UPPER_SNAKE_CASE

rules.description: Outside of true constants, every field, static or per-instance, is named in lowerCamelCase as a noun or noun phrase, static fields included.
rules.rationale: Keeping non-constant fields in lowerCamelCase rather than UPPER_SNAKE_CASE makes the constant/non-constant distinction visible from casing alone.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.5 (Non-constant field names)

_examples.explanation: instance field in lowerCamelCase

_examples.code: private static List<String> REGISTERED_NAMES = new ArrayList<>();
_examples.explanation: mutable static field is not a constant, so UPPER_SNAKE_CASE is wrong; should be registeredNames

rules.description: Parameters, whether on a method or a constructor, follow lowerCamelCase.
rules.rationale: Consistent camelCase for parameters matches local variables and keeps call sites readable.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.6 (Parameter names)

_examples.explanation: parameter name in lowerCamelCase
snake_case parameter name

rules.description: Public methods should not take parameters named with a single character; give each one a real word or short phrase instead.
rules.rationale: A single-letter name gives a caller of a public API no hint about what the argument represents.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.6 (Parameter names)

_examples.code: public void resize(int newWidth, int newHeight) { }
_examples.explanation: descriptive public-method parameter names

_examples.code: public void resize(int w, int h) { }
_examples.explanation: single-character parameter names on a public method

rules.description: Local variables are lowerCamelCase across the board. Marking one final and never reassigning it does not turn it into a constant, so it keeps ordinary camelCase rather than switching to UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
rules.rationale: Reserving UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for true constants keeps that casing a reliable signal, uncluttered by merely-final locals.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.7 (Local variable names)

_examples.explanation: final local variable still styled in lowerCamelCase, not as a constant
local variable incorrectly styled as if it were a constant

rules.description: A generic type parameter takes one of two shapes: a bare capital letter, with an optional trailing digit for a second parameter of a similar kind (as in a pair like K and K2); or, when a descriptive name is clearer, a class-like word ending in a capital 'T' (for example ResultT).
rules.rationale: A short, distinct visual form for type parameters keeps them from being mistaken for ordinary type or variable names.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.8 (Type variable names)

_examples.explanation: single-capital-letter type parameter
descriptive class-name-like form ending in capital T
lowercase full-word type parameter matches neither accepted form

rules.description: Not called out with its own example in the current text, but an enum constant is an implicitly static, final, immutable instance of its enum type, so it meets the general constant definition and is named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE like any other constant.
rules.rationale: Consistent with treating deeply-immutable static final values as constants regardless of how they are declared.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 5.2.4 (Constant names) — extrapolated, not a separate bullet

_examples.explanation: enum constants in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
enum constants in lowercase instead of UPPER_SNAKE_CASE

rules.triggerCondition: the class or interface is public (or otherwise part of the visible API), or is a protected member of a visible class
rules.description: At minimum, a Javadoc comment is present for every visible class or interface.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 7.3 (Where Javadoc is used)

_examples.code:
/** Generates PDF invoices from order data. */
public class InvoiceGenerator { }
_examples.explanation: public class has a Javadoc summary
public class has no Javadoc at all

rules.triggerCondition: the method is public or protected on a visible class, is not a simple/self-explanatory member with nothing worthwhile to add, and is not an override whose contract is already documented on the supertype method
rules.description: Public and protected methods on visible classes carry a Javadoc comment with, as applicable to the signature, a summary, @param entries, an @return entry and @throws entries — in that order, never left with an empty description. The rule relaxes for members simple enough that there is truly nothing else worth saying, and for overrides that inherit their documented contract.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 7.3, § 7.3.1, § 7.3.2 and § 7.1.3

_examples.code:
/**
 * Charges the given amount to the customer's default payment method.
 *
 * @param amount the amount to charge, in the account's currency
 * @return a receipt for the completed charge
 * @throws PaymentDeclinedException if the charge is rejected
 */
public Receipt charge(Money amount) throws PaymentDeclinedException { ... }
_examples.explanation: summary plus @param, @return and @throws in the correct order

_examples.code: public Receipt charge(Money amount) throws PaymentDeclinedException { ... }
_examples.explanation: public method with parameters and a checked exception has no Javadoc

rules.triggerCondition: the field is public or protected on a visible class
rules.description: Public or protected fields on visible classes carry at least a short Javadoc summary explaining what they represent.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 7.3 (Where Javadoc is used)

_examples.code:
/** Maximum number of retry attempts before giving up. */
public static final int MAX_RETRIES = 5;
_examples.explanation: public constant field has a Javadoc summary
public field has no Javadoc

rules.triggerCondition: any Javadoc block
rules.description: Every Javadoc block opens with a brief summary fragment — a noun phrase or verb phrase, not a full sentence, and not a restatement like 'A Foo is a...'. Despite being a fragment, it is still capitalized and ends with a period as if it were a complete sentence.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 7.2 (The summary fragment)

_examples.code: /** Returns the customer's current loyalty tier. */
_examples.explanation: terse verb-phrase summary fragment, capitalized and punctuated

_examples.code: /** This method returns the customer's current loyalty tier. */
_examples.explanation: written as a full sentence restating the obvious rather than a terse fragment

rules.triggerCondition: a Javadoc block contains more than one paragraph
rules.description:
When a Javadoc comment spans more than one paragraph, paragraphs are separated by a genuinely blank documentation line (a line with only the aligned leading asterisk in traditional Javadoc, or a blank line with a leading /// in Markdown Javadoc), and in traditional Javadoc each paragraph after the first opens with a

tag placed immediately before its first word.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 7.1.2 (Paragraphs)

_examples.code:
/** * Parses a currency string into a Money value. * *

Whitespace around the string is ignored. */
_examples.explanation: second paragraph separated by a blank doc line and opened with

_examples.code:
/**
 * Parses a currency string into a Money value.
 * Whitespace around the string is ignored.
 */
_examples.explanation:
second paragraph runs on with no blank line or

tag

rules.triggerCondition: a class, member or record component that is not part of the mandatory-Javadoc set (e.g. a private or package-private member)
rules.description: Beyond the mandatory minimum, classes, members and record components may carry Javadoc whenever the author finds it useful ('as needed or desired'); such non-required Javadoc is not strictly held to the formatting rules for general form, paragraphs, block-tag order or the summary-fragment rule, though following them anyway is recommended.
rules.sourceSection: Google Java Style Guide § 7.4 (Non-required Javadoc)

_examples.code:
/** Cache entries older than this are considered stale. */
private static final Duration STALE_AFTER = Duration.ofMinutes(10);
_examples.explanation: private field is not required to have Javadoc, but the author chose to add it anyway

rules.description: A class or struct is named with a noun or noun phrase, PascalCase throughout, and carries no artificial type marker; skip prefixes like a leading 'C' that some older C++ conventions used.
rules.rationale: A PascalCase noun reads as the thing the type represents; a Hungarian-style prefix like 'C' is redundant since the declaration already states it is a class.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

_examples.explanation: PascalCase noun phrase, no type prefix.
Adds a redundant 'C' type-indicator prefix.

rules.description: Interfaces are PascalCase adjectives or noun phrases carrying a capital 'I' at the front, and a class implementing one is usually named identically minus that leading 'I' (an interface ISerializer typically has a concrete implementation simply called Serializer).
rules.rationale: The 'I' prefix lets a reader distinguish an interface reference from a class reference at a glance, and keeps the interface/implementation pair visually linked.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

_examples.explanation: Adjective-free noun phrase prefixed with 'I'.
Missing the 'I' prefix that marks this as an interface.

rules.description: A method's name is PascalCase and centers on a verb or verb phrase that names the action it carries out.
rules.rationale: Methods do something; a verb-led name makes call sites read like instructions rather than noun lookups.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Type Members

_examples.code: public decimal CalculateTotal() { return LineItems.Sum(i => i.Price); }
_examples.explanation: PascalCase verb phrase describing the action.

_examples.code: public decimal TotalCalculation() { return LineItems.Sum(i => i.Price); }
_examples.explanation: Noun phrase instead of a verb phrase.

rules.description: Properties take PascalCase names built from a noun, noun phrase, or adjective. A property backed by a collection should be pluralized on its own (Orders, not OrderList), and no property should share its exact name with a Get-prefixed method on the same type.
rules.rationale: Properties represent state, so noun-shaped names read naturally as 'object.Attribute'; a plural collection name avoids implying the property itself is a single item.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Type Members

_examples.explanation: Plural noun for a collection-valued property.
Singular name plus a redundant 'List' suffix instead of a plural noun.

rules.description: A public or protected field gets the same PascalCase noun-phrase treatment as a property, with no scope-marking prefix tacked on (skip legacy conventions like a leading 'g' or 's' to flag global or static storage). Private and internal field casing is a choice this guideline leaves open.
rules.rationale: Public fields are part of the API surface and should follow the same PascalCase convention as properties and methods so the surface reads consistently.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Type Members

_examples.code: public static readonly TimeSpan DefaultTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
_examples.explanation: PascalCase public field with no scope prefix.

_examples.code: public static readonly TimeSpan s_DefaultTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
_examples.explanation: Uses a Hungarian-style 's_' scope prefix on a public field.

rules.description: Choose a parameter name that describes what the value means, not what type it is, and use camelCase. The one carve-out is an operator-overload parameter that has no natural name of its own: use generic placeholders such as 'first'/'second' for a two-operand operator or 'operand' for a one-operand operator, rather than an abbreviation or a numbered index.
rules.rationale: A descriptive camelCase parameter name doubles as inline documentation at every call site that uses named arguments or shows IntelliSense.
rules.sourceSection: Naming Parameters

_examples.code: public decimal ConvertCurrency(decimal amount, string targetCurrencyCode) { ... }
_examples.explanation: Descriptive camelCase parameter names.

_examples.code: public decimal ConvertCurrency(decimal a, string s) { ... }
_examples.explanation: Single-letter, non-descriptive parameter names.

rules.description: Namespaces are dot-separated PascalCase segments that generally widen from an organization identifier down to more specific areas, something like Organization, then a product or technology area, then an optional feature and sub-area, rather than mirroring an internal team or org-chart structure; a namespace should never reuse the exact name of a type defined within it, or vice versa.
rules.rationale: A company/product-rooted, PascalCase-dotted namespace avoids collisions across vendors and stays stable even when internal teams are reorganized.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Namespaces

_examples.explanation: PascalCase, dot-separated Company.Product.Feature pattern.
snake_case component and lowercase instead of PascalCase-dotted.

rules.description: A plain enum type takes a singular PascalCase name; once it's marked with [Flags] so members can be OR-combined, switch to a plural PascalCase name instead.
rules.rationale: Singular vs. plural signals at the declaration whether a variable of that enum type holds exactly one value or a combinable set of values.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

_examples.explanation: Singular name for a non-flags enum.
Plural name used for a non-flags (single-value) enum.

rules.description: Skip appending words like 'Enum', 'Flag', or 'Flags' onto an enum type's own name; the enum keyword and an optional [Flags] attribute already make that clear without repeating it in the identifier.
rules.rationale: The suffix is redundant metadata the type system already expresses, and it makes names longer without adding information.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

_examples.explanation: No redundant 'Enum' suffix.
Adds a literal 'Enum' suffix to the type name.

rules.description: Enum members are PascalCase with no coded prefix tying them back to their containing enum; avoid an old-style abbreviation prefix the way some early COM-era APIs tagged every member of an enum with a short code.
rules.rationale: The member is always accessed through its enum type (EnumType.Member), so a per-member type prefix is redundant and adds noise.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

_examples.explanation: PascalCase members with no coded prefix.
Legacy-style 'cs' abbreviation prefix on each member.

rules.description: A generic type parameter's name usually starts with a capital 'T' followed by something descriptive, and echoing a constraint it must satisfy is a good source for that description. When there's only one type parameter and its role is obvious from context, the bare letter 'T' on its own is acceptable.
rules.rationale: The 'T' prefix marks the identifier as a type parameter rather than an ordinary type name at a glance, while still allowing a descriptive name when a type has more than one parameter.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

_examples.explanation: Descriptive type parameters prefixed with 'T'.
Type parameters omit the required 'T' prefix.

rules.description: Name constants — both const fields and local constants — in PascalCase regardless of their access modifier, so public, internal, and private constants are all cased the same way.
rules.rationale: Keeping constant casing independent of visibility avoids a name having to change if its access modifier later changes, and keeps constants visually distinct from camelCase locals.
rules.sourceSection: C# identifier naming rules and conventions — Constants

_examples.explanation: PascalCase constant regardless of its private visibility.
snake_case instead of PascalCase for a constant.

rules.description: Local variables are camelCase with names clear enough that a reader doesn't have to guess their purpose; favor a few extra characters of clarity over brevity, except for a throwaway loop index where a single letter is fine.
rules.rationale: camelCase visually distinguishes a local variable from PascalCase types and members declared in the same scope, and a descriptive name reduces the need to trace a variable back to its declaration to understand it.
rules.sourceSection: C# identifier naming rules and conventions — Local variables

_examples.explanation: camelCase, descriptive local variable name.
PascalCase used for a local variable, which reads like a type member.

rules.description: State a boolean identifier's positive case rather than its negative one, preferring a name that reads true for the common, expected condition, and, when a prefix would clarify things further, common choices include forms like 'Is', 'Can', or 'Has'. As with any member, casing still follows whether it's a local (camelCase) or a public member (PascalCase).
rules.rationale: A negatively phrased boolean forces a double negative at every use site (e.g. '!NotConnected'), which is easy to misread; an affirmative name with an optional Is/Can/Has prefix reads directly as a yes/no question.
rules.sourceSection: Names of Type Members; C# identifier naming rules and conventions

_examples.code: public bool IsConnected { get; private set; }
_examples.explanation: Affirmative phrasing with an 'Is' prefix.

_examples.code: public bool NotConnected { get; private set; }
_examples.explanation: Negative phrasing forces double negatives like '!NotConnected'.

rules.description: Skip Hungarian-notation prefixes that spell out a variable's type in miniature (things like 'str', 'i', or 'b' tacked onto the front of a name), and don't rely on underscores or other punctuation to break up words inside an identifier.
rules.rationale: Modern tooling shows a variable's declared type on hover, so an encoded type prefix only adds clutter and can go stale if the type changes; PascalCase/camelCase word boundaries already remove the need for separators.
rules.sourceSection: General Naming Conventions; Capitalization Conventions

_examples.explanation: Plain descriptive camelCase, no type-coded prefix.
Hungarian-notation 'str' type prefix on the variable name.

rules.triggerCondition: A class, struct, interface, or enum is declared with public or protected visibility.
rules.description: Give every publicly visible type an XML doc comment with at least a <summary> element describing what it represents; documenting private types is optional.
rules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — General tags

_examples.explanation: Public class carries a <summary> XML doc comment.
Public class has no XML doc comment at all.

rules.triggerCondition: A public or protected method is declared; a <param> element is expected for each declared parameter, and a <returns> element is expected when the method's return type is not void.
rules.description: Document every public/protected method with a <summary>, one <param> tag per parameter, and a <returns> tag describing the return value when the method returns one; the C# compiler warns when a method's <param> tags do not match its actual parameter list.
rules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Member tags

_examples.explanation: Summary plus a <param> for the parameter and a <returns> for the result.
Missing <param> for 'percentage' and <returns> for the result.

rules.triggerCondition: A public or protected property is declared.
rules.description: Document every public/protected property with a <summary>, and add a <value> element describing what the property represents; Visual Studio's generated property doc template includes <value> by default.
rules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Member tags

_examples.explanation: Summary plus a <value> describing the property's meaning.

rules.triggerCondition: A public generic type or generic method declares one or more type parameters.
rules.description: Document each type parameter of a public generic type or method with a <typeparam name="..."> element; the compiler verifies that documented type-parameter names match the declaration.
rules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Generic type documentation

_examples.explanation: Every generic type parameter has a matching <typeparam> tag.

rules.triggerCondition: A public/protected method throws an exception as part of its documented, expected contract (e.g., it validates an argument and throws on failure).
rules.description: Where a public/protected method can throw an exception as part of its contract, add an <exception cref="..."> element naming the exception type and describing the condition that triggers it.
rules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Member tags

_examples.explanation: Documents the specific exception the method can throw and why.

rules.triggerCondition: A member of a publicly visible enum type is declared.
rules.description: Give each member of a publicly visible enum its own <summary> XML doc comment describing what that value represents, consistent with the general guidance to document all publicly visible types and members.
rules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — When to apply XML documentation comments

_examples.explanation: Each public enum member has its own <summary>.

rules.description: Class names use UpperCamelCase (PascalCase).
rules.rationale: Consistent casing lets readers recognize a declaration's kind from its name alone.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: class

_examples.explanation: Class name uses UpperCamelCase.
snake_case instead of UpperCamelCase.

rules.description: Interface names use UpperCamelCase, the same as classes; do not prefix an interface with 'I' or otherwise decorate the name to mark it as an interface — name it for what it represents.
rules.rationale: Names should not carry redundant type information; TypeScript's type system already distinguishes interfaces from classes.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifiers / Naming style

_examples.explanation: UpperCamelCase name with no interface marker prefix.
Leading 'I' decorates the name with redundant type information.

rules.description: A type parameter's name can simply be one capital letter (T, U, or similar), or, when extra clarity helps, a complete descriptive name written in UpperCamelCase.
rules.rationale: Short generics stay terse for simple containers while descriptive names aid readability when a type parameter's role isn't obvious.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: type parameters

_examples.explanation: Single uppercase letter T for a simple generic container.
Descriptive UpperCamelCase type parameter, also acceptable.

rules.description: Functions use lowerCamelCase, and an acronym inside the name is capitalized like an ordinary word rather than left in all caps (write parseJsonBody, not parseJSONBody), with narrow exceptions where an external platform interface's exact spelling must be preserved as-is.
rules.rationale: Uniform camelCase capitalization of acronyms keeps names visually consistent and avoids ambiguous runs of capitals.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: functions / Descriptive names

_examples.explanation: camelCase name treats the HTTP/URL acronyms as ordinary words.
Acronyms left in all caps break the camelCase pattern.

rules.description: Method names use lowerCamelCase, the same convention as functions and variables.
rules.rationale: Keeps callable members visually consistent across classes and modules.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: methods

_examples.explanation: Method name uses lowerCamelCase.
snake_case method name.

rules.description: Variables, local or module-scoped, are lowerCamelCase and never bracketed by underscores. Skip abbreviations a newcomer to the codebase wouldn't recognize; a single letter is only acceptable when the variable's whole lifetime fits in a couple of lines.
rules.rationale: Underscore decoration and cryptic abbreviations obscure meaning instead of encoding it in the name itself.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: variables / Descriptive names

_examples.explanation: lowerCamelCase variable with no underscore decoration.
Leading underscore is disallowed.

rules.description: CONSTANT_CASE is for a value that is both genuinely global and genuinely immutable: a module-scope constant, a static readonly field on a class defined at module scope, or an enum member. The moment a 'constant' can exist as more than one instance, such as a const declared inside a function body or a static field on a locally-scoped class, it drops back to lowerCamelCase regardless of its own immutability.
rules.rationale: CONSTANT_CASE signals module-wide, singleton-like immutability; reserving it for genuinely global values keeps the signal meaningful.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: constants / Global constant names

_examples.explanation: Module-level immutable global uses CONSTANT_CASE.
Module-level global constant written in camelCase instead of CONSTANT_CASE.

rules.description: Parameter names use lowerCamelCase. Do not prefix an optional parameter with opt_; express optionality with TypeScript's ? syntax or a default value instead.
rules.rationale: TypeScript's own optional-parameter syntax already conveys optionality, making an opt_ prefix redundant type decoration.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifiers / Naming style

_examples.code: function resize(width: number, height?: number): void {}
_examples.explanation: Optional parameter uses TypeScript's ? syntax, no opt_ prefix.

_examples.code: function resize(width: number, opt_height?: number): void {}
_examples.explanation: opt_ prefix redundantly decorates an already-optional parameter.

rules.description: Class fields use lowerCamelCase. Do not signal visibility with a leading/trailing underscore or the native #private syntax; use the private/protected/public/readonly modifiers instead.
rules.rationale: Visibility is already expressed by TypeScript's access modifiers, so underscore or # decoration is redundant and inconsistent across a codebase.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifiers / Naming style

_examples.explanation: Private field uses lowerCamelCase and the private modifier for visibility.
Leading underscore duplicates what the private modifier already says.

rules.description: Object and interface properties use lowerCamelCase, consistent with class fields and variables.
rules.rationale: A single casing convention for data members keeps object shapes and class shapes visually interchangeable.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: properties

_examples.explanation: Properties named in lowerCamelCase.
PascalCase-with-underscore property names.

rules.description: Enum type names use UpperCamelCase, the same as classes and interfaces.
rules.rationale: An enum introduces a new type, so it follows the same casing convention as other type declarations.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: enums

_examples.explanation: Enum type name uses UpperCamelCase.
snake_case enum type name.

rules.description: Enum members use CONSTANT_CASE, since each member is effectively a global constant value.
rules.rationale: Enum values behave like named constants at every call site, so they take the constant naming convention.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: enums / Global constant names

_examples.explanation: Enum members use CONSTANT_CASE.
Enum members written in lowercase instead of CONSTANT_CASE.

rules.description: When importing an entire module under a namespace alias (import * as fooBar from './foo_bar'), the alias is lowerCamelCase regardless of how the source file itself is named. A small set of long-standing third-party aliasing conventions, such as a dollar sign for jQuery or an all-caps namespace for a library like three.js, can be kept rather than forced into camelCase.
rules.rationale: Aliasing a module binds it to an ordinary identifier, so it follows the ordinary variable/module casing rule rather than the file-naming convention.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Naming — Identifier type: module aliases

_examples.explanation: Namespace import alias uses lowerCamelCase even though the file is snake_case.
PascalCase alias instead of lowerCamelCase.

rules.triggerCondition: The declaration (function, class, constant, type, etc.) is exported at the top level of a module.
rules.description: Every symbol exported from the top level of a module must carry a JSDoc comment describing what it does, so a consumer of the module can understand it without reading its implementation.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Comments and Documentation — JSDoc general form

_examples.explanation: Top-level exported function carries a JSDoc summary.
Exported function has no JSDoc at all.

rules.triggerCondition: A class is declared, particularly one that is exported.
rules.description: Class-level JSDoc should describe the class's purpose, how and when to use it, and any special considerations; the constructor itself typically needs no separate description when its behavior is obvious from its parameters.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Comments and Documentation — Class comments

_examples.explanation: Class JSDoc explains purpose and timing behavior.

rules.triggerCondition: A method or function's behavior, parameters, or return value are not obvious from its name and type signature alone.
rules.description: A method whose behavior isn't self-evident gets a short summary phrased as a verb, plus @param/@return entries where they contribute something. Skip a parameter or return description, or the whole comment, once the name and type signature already say the same thing.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Comments and Documentation — Method and function comments

_examples.explanation: Non-obvious method documented with summary, @param, and @return.

rules.triggerCondition: A constructor parameter is declared with a private/protected/public/readonly modifier (a TypeScript 'parameter property').
rules.description: Constructor parameter properties must be documented with an @param tag, each on its own line, because TypeScript collapses the parameter and the field declaration into a single line that leaves nowhere else to describe them.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Comments and Documentation — Parameter property comments

_examples.explanation: Parameter properties documented with @param tags, one per line.
Parameter properties left undocumented.

rules.triggerCondition: Any comment is written in the source, whether documenting an API or explaining implementation detail.
rules.description: Keep the two comment styles doing different jobs: JSDoc blocks (/** */) are for tool-parseable, user-facing documentation, while plain // lines cover implementation notes aimed at future maintainers. When an implementation note runs long, stack several // lines rather than switching to a /* */ block, and never wrap a comment in a border of asterisks.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Comments and Documentation — JSDoc vs. non-JSDoc comments

_examples.explanation: JSDoc documents the public API; a // line comment explains an internal detail.
Decorative asterisk-boxed block comment instead of JSDoc or line comments.

rules.triggerCondition: A JSDoc comment contains formatted content, such as a list.
rules.description: Tooling renders JSDoc text as Markdown, not as preformatted text, so a bulleted list inside a doc comment needs an actual Markdown dash rather than just extra indentation, or the generated docs will show it as a single run-on paragraph.
rules.sourceSection: Google TypeScript Style Guide § Comments and Documentation — Markdown

_examples.explanation: List uses Markdown dash syntax so it renders correctly.
Plain indentation instead of Markdown list syntax will not render as a list.

rules.description: Avoid single-letter variable names; choose names descriptive enough that they communicate what the value represents.
rules.rationale: A single letter gives a reader no clue about intent, forcing them to trace usage to understand the code.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.1 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: descriptive variable name
single-letter name gives no context

rules.description: Avoid single-letter parameter names; a parameter's name should describe what is passed in.
rules.rationale: Same descriptive-naming rationale as general identifiers, applied to function parameters (the guide's id-length reference is not kind-specific).
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.1 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: parameter name describes what is passed in
single-letter parameter name

rules.description: Give ordinary variables and instances of a class the standard camelCase treatment.
rules.rationale: camelCase is the guide's baseline casing for ordinary bindings, keeping identifiers consistent across a codebase.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.2 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: camelCase variable
snake_case instead of camelCase

rules.description: Functions, like variables, are named in camelCase.
rules.rationale: Distinguishes ordinary callables from constructors/classes, which use PascalCase instead.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.2 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: camelCase function name
PascalCase used for a plain function, not a constructor

rules.description: Name object and class methods in camelCase, the same as standalone functions.
rules.rationale: Methods are functions attached to an object/class, so the same camelCase rule applies.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.2 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: camelCase method name
PascalCase used for a method

rules.description: Reserve PascalCase for the names of classes and the functions used as constructors.
rules.rationale: Reserving PascalCase for constructors/classes lets a reader tell at a glance that a name must be invoked with `new`.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.3 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: PascalCase class name
camelCase used for a class

rules.description: Leading or trailing underscores on an instance field are not used as a signal of privacy; there's no enforcement benefit, so skip the convention.
rules.rationale: JavaScript (pre-# private fields) has no real property privacy, so a leading/trailing underscore is a misleading convention rather than an enforced guarantee.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.4 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: plain field name, no underscore
leading underscore falsely implies privacy

rules.description: Keep object property/key names in camelCase, including the nested keys of an object whose own exported binding is written in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
rules.rationale: Uppercasing is reserved for the exported constant identifier itself, not for the properties nested inside it, so property keys stay camelCase throughout.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.2, § 23.10 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: camelCase property keys
snake_case and PascalCase keys instead of camelCase

rules.description: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for a constant is allowed, but only under three conditions at once: it's declared with const so it can never be reassigned, it's exported for use elsewhere, and neither it nor anything nested inside it is expected to ever change.
rules.rationale: Uppercasing signals true, trustworthy immutability to any consumer of the export; using it elsewhere would be a false signal.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.10 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: exported, const, guaranteed-immutable value
uppercased but declared with let, so it can be reassigned

rules.description: Do not uppercase a constant that is only used locally within a file; UPPER_SNAKE_CASE is reserved for exported, truly-immutable constants.
rules.rationale: Uppercasing every local constant adds visual noise without conveying any additional guarantee, since local constants are not part of a public contract.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.10 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: local, unexported constant kept in camelCase
uppercased even though it is only used locally in the file

rules.description: When a file's default export is something class-like, such as a constructor, a class itself, a singleton instance, a namespace of related functions, or a plain object used as one, name that export in PascalCase and make sure the file it lives in shares that exact name.
rules.rationale: Matching the filename to the export makes the exported symbol discoverable from the file system alone.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.6, § 23.8 Naming Conventions

_examples.code:
// file: PaymentProcessor.js
export default class PaymentProcessor { }
_examples.explanation: filename matches PascalCase default class export

_examples.code:
// file: paymentProcessor.js
export default class PaymentProcessor { }
_examples.explanation: filename casing does not match the exported class name

rules.description: When the default export is instead a single function, camelCase applies to both the export's name and the filename, and the two should match exactly.
rules.rationale: Same filename-matches-export rationale as class exports, applied to the camelCase casing used for functions.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.6, § 23.7 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: filename matches camelCase default function export
kebab-case filename does not match the camelCase export name

rules.description: Pick one casing convention for an acronym embedded in an identifier and hold to it everywhere: either spell it out in full capitals or treat it like an ordinary word, instead of mixing the two conventions in the same name (an HTTP client class should be HttpClient or HTTPClient, not a mixed form).
rules.rationale: Mixed-case acronyms are ambiguous to read and inconsistent to type; picking one convention keeps names predictable.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 23.9 Naming Conventions

_examples.explanation: acronym SMS is fully uppercase, consistently applied
acronym is mixed-case (Sms) instead of fully upper or fully lower

rules.description: A boolean-returning accessor's name may optionally lead with a verb like is or has (as in isActive() or hasName()) to make its truthy return value obvious. Airbnb frames this as encouraged style rather than a strict requirement, so treat it as a strong recommendation, not a hard rule.
rules.rationale: The prefix makes the method read as a yes/no question at the call site, signalling its boolean return type without checking the implementation.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 24.3 Accessors

_examples.explanation: boolean accessor method prefixed with is
boolean accessor method has no is/has prefix

rules.description: By extension of Airbnb's boolean-accessor convention, prefix boolean variables with is or has so the name reads as a yes/no question (e.g. isVisible, hasPermission).
rules.rationale: Same readability rationale as the accessor-method rule; applying it to boolean variables keeps naming consistent across kinds. Note: the guide states this explicitly only for accessor properties/methods (§24.3), not for plain boolean variable declarations — this rule is an inferred extension, rated lower accordingly.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 24.3 Accessors (extended)

_examples.explanation: boolean variable prefixed with has
boolean variable name reads as a noun, not a yes/no question

rules.triggerCondition: a comment spans multiple lines, such as documentation above a function, class, or block
rules.description: For a comment spanning several lines, use the /** ... */ block form instead of piling up consecutive // lines.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 18.1 Comments

_examples.explanation: multiline doc comment uses /** */ block syntax
stacked // lines used instead of a /** */ block for a multiline comment

requiredElements: blank line before it (unless first line of a block)
rules.triggerCondition: a short explanatory comment about the statement(s) that follow
rules.description: A single-line comment uses //, sits on its own line immediately above whatever it explains, and is set off from the code above it by a blank line, except when it opens a block, where no blank line is needed.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 18.2 Comments

_examples.explanation: comment on its own line, blank line before it
missing blank line before the comment

requiredElements: single leading space after the comment marker
rules.triggerCondition: any // or /** */ comment
rules.description: Leave exactly one space between the comment marker, // or the opening /**, and the text that follows it, for every comment in the codebase.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 18.3 Comments (eslint: spaced-comment)

_examples.explanation: space after the // marker
no space after the // marker

rules.triggerCondition: a known problem in the code that needs to be revisited or investigated
rules.description: Annotate a known problem with a `// FIXME:` prefixed comment so it is easy to find and search for later.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 18.4-18.5 Comments

_examples.code: // FIXME: throws when the cart is empty
_examples.explanation: known problem flagged with FIXME prefix

_examples.code: // this breaks when the cart is empty, need to fix
_examples.explanation: known problem noted without the FIXME marker

rules.triggerCondition: a solution or enhancement that is known but not yet implemented
rules.description: Annotate planned-but-unimplemented work with a `// TODO:` prefixed comment.
rules.sourceSection: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide § 18.4, § 18.6 Comments
